inline.s: The governor Liu Kun had not cultivated the Way or realized sagehood; it was simply by a single thought of benevolence that he was at once able to quell a raging tiger menace — how much more so for one who learns the compassion of the Buddha! Again, take the case of enlightened holy monks who tamed tigers and subdued dragons, and of the modern ‘tiger-taming monk,’ the Elder Guangqin — his deeds too are familiar to everyone, and were even witnessed with their own eyes; they are by no means fabrications. If everyone could learn from the Buddha and from the holy monks, then even if fierce and cruel beasts such as tigers and leopards filled the world, they could do no harm! Why then worry that birds and beasts will injure people? For when violent men are all transformed into the compassionate, the beasts that harm people are likewise transformed into qilin and phoenixes! Hence we know that though some creatures are exceedingly fierce and venomous, there is still a place where they may be moved and transformed — the only fear is that we ourselves may fail to be compassionate!
To dig out the insects that lie dormant in the earth, and to disturb the birds roosting in the trees.

When the weather turns cold, the insects all lie dormant in the earth; if they are dug out, they will surely freeze stiff and die. Therefore the Most High wrote this out here especially, to forbid people from doing so; and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas in particular cherish and pity these small insects. How can people fail to take this principle to heart, and carelessly dig out the insects that lie dormant in the earth?

The great Song general Cao Bin would never repair his houses or walls in wintertime. Someone asked him why. Cao Bin replied, ‘To repair house walls in winter would likely injure the insects lying dormant inside!’

Cao Bin and his grandsons were enfeoffed as kings by the emperors generation after generation; such was the greatness of his blessings. Yet he was unwilling to plant the evil cause of digging out dormant insects. And now there are people who wantonly burn mountains, forests, and grass, and even dare to make a game and amusement of it, giving free rein to a moment’s pleasure while injuring billions of living creatures. Why do we not take the story of Cao Bin’s care for dormant insects and warn and remind one another by it? If we come upon someone burning grass, woods, or mountains, we should put the fire out at once; and as for villagers and children who do such things out of ignorance, we should especially counsel them well. If someone pours hot water on the ground, or burns paper money on the earth as an offering to the ancestors, in all these cases we should give timely attention and gentle counsel, so as to preserve the dormant insects beneath the ground from harm. Such a mind is truly most compassionate!

Since the birds have already settled in the trees, it is just as when a person has already gone to bed and fallen asleep; if at such a time one suddenly startles and disturbs them, would not the whole household be thrown into confusion? The Most High’s admonition not to disturb the birds roosting in the trees is the same in meaning as Confucius’s saying, ‘He would not shoot a bird at roost.’ The Scripture of the Immortals likewise says, ‘Whoever is able to practice skillful means at any time and in any place to save and protect the lives of living beings will surely receive the reward of merit and long life.’

Long ago there was an old woman who lived in the mountains, named Li Xizi. Whenever the great snows came, the branches of the trees were all covered with snow, so that the birds had no place to roost; they came flying to gather at her house, and the old woman would feed them grain, not daring to startle them. The Lord on High said, ‘Li Xizi has a benevolent heart; she may live to be five hundred years old.’ And in the end Li Xizi truly lived to be five hundred.

There was a man surnamed Yang who made his living by catching birds and selling them for money. One day he saw a winter magpie roosting on a branch, so he took a bamboo pole smeared with glue and climbed the branch to catch it. The branch broke and he fell from the tree; the pole he was holding in his hand pierced his head, and he bled to death.
To stop up the burrows where insects and ants live, and to overturn the nests where birds roost.

A burrow is the gathering place of all the tiny creatures that hold a spirit. From a human’s point of view it is merely a hole in the ground; from their point of view it is the home on which they depend for shelter. It is no different from the home a person lives in — how can one fill up and stop such a burrow? To do so is to cut off their gate of life, block their way out, and even wipe out their whole clan! How can human beings bear to do such a thing!

Formerly there was a bhiksu who had attained the six spiritual powers through cultivation and lived together with a young novice monk. In his meditative concentration the bhiksu saw that the novice had only seven days left to live; so he found a convenient pretext and told the novice to go home and visit his parents. Eight days later the novice returned, alive. The bhiksu was astonished, and entering concentration again he observed: why had the novice not died? Then he understood. On the road home the novice had seen an anthill, and the water running over the ground was about to flow into the ants’ hole. The novice hurriedly took off his robe, and with earth he dammed the water so that it could not flow into the ants’ burrow. Because of this cause of saving the ants’ lives, the novice’s lifespan was extended by twelve years; and for this reason he practiced even more diligently and attained the fruit of the fourth-stage arhat.

In Hangzhou there was a woman who delighted in killing living creatures, and above all hated ants for dirtying her food. So she often burned ants to death; whenever she found an anthill, she either stopped it up or poured boiling water into it, killing countless ants. Later she bore a child, still at the nursing stage; one day this child was bitten all over by a great swarm of ants until his whole body swelled up, and in the end his flesh rotted and he died.

Mr. Zhu Ji said, ‘A woman loves her child as she loves her own life; so when urging a woman to abstain from killing, one should use this case to persuade her — it is more effective, for the woman being urged will feel afraid.’ Therefore in Zhu Ji’s vow to abstain from killing there are the two lines, ‘If I raise the knife again, it is as though I were killing our own children’ — on the one hand to caution himself, and on the other to caution his wife.

A nest is the place where birds of every size rely for shelter while they suckle and give birth, and where they can also escape the onslaught of frost and snow and the danger of being caught in nets or struck by pellets. If someone overturns a bird’s nest, it is no different from a human being whose house is destroyed and whose home is burned — is that not to put them to death? The Most High says in the Chapter on Preserving One’s Offspring: ‘Whenever a person’s descendants decline and are cut off, it is because in a former life he overturned birds’ nests, destroyed birds’ eggs, burned mountains and forests for hunting, drained ponds to catch fish, or caused abortions and destroyed children, thus violating the one thousand six hundred and twentieth precept; and only for this reason does he bring down upon himself the retribution of his descendants being cut off.’

The Buddha said, ‘If you see someone climbing a tree to take birds’ eggs, or entering the water to catch fish, then you should silently recite the holy name of Ratnasikhin Tathagata several dozen times, and the eggs and the fish will thereby escape their calamity. This too is a way of saving lives.’ Someone may ask, ‘One ought first to be kind to people and afterward to love creatures; why is it that now people are taught only to love creatures — what is the reason for this?’ We should answer, ‘Because being kind to people is comparatively easy, while loving creatures is comparatively difficult. If a person dares to harden his heart and harm creatures, then he will surely also dare to harden his heart and harm people; and if a person cannot bear to harm creatures, then his heart toward others may be known as well.’ Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra says, ‘I cannot even bear to make an ant do hard labor; how much less a human being!’

In ancient times King Tang, the founder of the Shang, himself taught a hunter to spread his net on three sides only, so as not to take all the game at one cast; his benevolent heart moved the hunter deeply. King Tang extended this heart that loved creatures to the common people, and so his benevolence covered all the living beings under heaven. Once King Xuan of Qi could not bear to see an ox trembling with fear as it was led past the hall, looking as though it had committed no crime yet was being taken unjustly to its death; so he ordered a sheep to be substituted for it. The common people, however, misunderstood, thinking that King Xuan begrudged an ox and used a small sheep to replace a big one; but Mencius praised King Xuan for having a benevolent heart sufficient to practice kingly government, and said that if King Xuan could extend that heart, he would be able to keep the empire. Had Bai Qi, the great general of Qin, been able to hold a heart that loved creatures, he would not have buried alive four hundred thousand soldiers of Zhao at the battle of Changping! So loving creatures and loving people are one and the same benevolent heart. When the Tathagata was practicing on the causal ground, out of pity for a dove pursued by a hawk he protected the dove; and the hawk reproached the Buddha for being too cruel, since in saving the dove he would let the hawk starve to death. Thereupon the Buddha cut flesh from his own arm to feed the hawk, without the least regret in his mind; and at once the flesh on his arm grew back again. The Buddha’s great compassion and great pity in giving his arm’s flesh to the hawk not only filled the ten directions but overflowed throughout ten thousand kalpas. Who says that one who loves creatures cannot love people? Therefore one who can save beings from suffering with every thought is a manifestation of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara; and one who can practice kindness with every thought is Bodhisattva Maitreya descending to be born in the world!

In the Song dynasty Su Shi built a dwelling at Dongpo and lived there, and so he called himself the Layman of Dongpo. In front of his study he planted many bamboos, cypresses, flowers, and grasses; in time the whole courtyard was filled with bamboo, cypress, flowers, and grass, and many birds came to build nests in the trees before his house. Dongpo therefore forbade his children and servants to catch the birds; and after a few years the nests the birds built on the branches were made lower and lower, so that even with the head bowed one could see the eggs in the nests!

I have heard it said of old that birds build their nests close to human dwellings, for the very purpose of keeping away from the harm of snakes, rats, and hawks. Yet people today go so far as to eat their fledglings and overturn the nests they have built — are human beings then less compassionate than snakes, rats, and hawks?

In the Song dynasty there was a man surnamed Zhu who liked to overturn birds’ nests and especially hated bees. Whenever he saw a bees’ nest, even if it was built in a very high place, he would find a way, bring a ladder, climb up, and destroy it. Later he had two sons; when the children were born, their anuses were blocked, so that they could not excrete, and before long they died. Mr. Zhu in the end was left without descendants.

The Chan master Cishou said: ‘Men take much life; hence come the sword-swept years. You took a life — your own life disappears. You owed a debt — your house is burned to clay. You broke a nest — your wife is torn away. Each deed its own exact requital earns; so wash your ears, and of the Buddha learn.’ The meaning of this verse is: ‘The many killings of the people of the world are the cause, and so there is the retribution of the kalpas of sword and soldier. Because you killed another’s life, he comes to kill you, demanding that you repay his life. Because you owed another’s money and did not repay it, he comes to burn your house and make you lose your property. Your wife and children are scattered from you because in the past you destroyed the nests and burrows of birds and bees — this is retribution. And the retribution is exactly matched; so we should wash our ears and listen well to what the Buddha says!’
To injure the unborn young of animals and to destroy their eggs is the act of killing.

Though the birds and beasts have not yet been born, the womb and the egg both contain life, just as when a human being is with child; so to injure their young and destroy their eggs is nothing other than to kill. The Buddha said, ‘If a person is fierce and cruel, not believing in the principle of cause and effect, and dares to catch newly hatched fledglings and eat their eggs, causing the birds to lose their young and cry out in grief, even to the point of weeping blood from their eyes, such a person will receive the retribution of being lonely and without a son.’

Formerly Bai Guinian went into the mountains to seek the immortals and study the Way, and obtained a book of the immortals; by it he learned to understand the speech of every kind of bird and beast. One day as he passed through Luzhou, the governor learned that he had this special ability, and so invited him to come and sit with him. It happened that the governor’s subordinates were driving a flock of sheep past the courtyard; among them was one sheep that would not move no matter how it was whipped, and that kept bleating pitifully. Seeing this, the governor asked Bai Guinian, ‘Master Bai, can you tell what this sheep is saying?’ Bai Guinian replied, ‘This sheep says that it is with young and about to give birth; when it has given birth, it will be willing to die.’ The governor, greatly amazed, ordered his subordinates to keep the sheep and not kill it; and before long the sheep indeed gave birth to two lambs.

Emperor Wenzong of the Tang dynasty paid great attention to food. Once, while the imperial kitchen was boiling eggs for him, there suddenly came from within the pot a faint sound, as though a multitude were crying out together the holy name of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and the sound was exceedingly mournful and sad. The officer supervising the kitchen reported the matter to the emperor, and the emperor sent people to inspect the kitchen, and it was indeed so. The emperor sighed and said, ‘I did not know that the awesome spiritual power of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas could respond in such a way!’ Thereupon he ordered that from that day on no more eggs should be boiled.

We should know that to save beings from suffering and distress is the original vow-power of Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara. Even the eggs boiling in a pot could cry out together the holy name of the Bodhisattva — how then can we human beings fail to recite the Bodhisattva’s holy name with reverence?

In the Liang dynasty there was a man who washed his hair with egg white mixed with water, in order to make his hair black and glossy; for this he broke many eggs. As he lay dying, he heard from within his hair the chirping of several thousand chicks.
Always to wish others failure and to take delight in their calamities.

When another person meets with failure, it is truly a most unfortunate matter; not to grieve for him and pity him, but instead to wish that he fail utterly — this is what is called rejoicing in another’s calamity. Since such a person considers calamity something to be rejoiced in, how could calamity fail to follow after him? Then the failure will not belong to another, but will fall upon himself. However foolish a person may be, he should not do such a thing!

Li Shiheng was ordered to go on a mission to Goryeo, and Yu Ying served as his deputy, accompanying him on that mission. All the gifts Li Shiheng received he handed over to Yu Ying to handle. Yu Ying, fearing that there would be dampness when the ship crossed the sea, put all of Li Shiheng’s gifts at the bottom of the ship and placed his own goods on top. Unexpectedly they met a great wind in mid-voyage, and the boatmen asked that the ship’s cargo be lightened to ensure the safety of the people and the vessel; so in the hurry and confusion many goods were thrown overboard at random. When the wind stopped, they checked what had just been thrown away: it was all Yu Ying’s things. And of Li Shiheng’s gifts, because they were all at the bottom of the ship, not a single one was lost.
Who does not have a selfish thought like Yu Ying’s? It is simply that because one’s own mind cannot be impartial, in the end one harms oneself!

The Nirvana Sutra says, ‘A practitioner should, by the power of wisdom, apply the six methods impartially in order to subdue his own mind; he must cause his mind, in its application, to be equal in all things.’ (The six methods are: conduct of body, conduct of speech, conduct of mind, rightful gain and support, upholding the precepts, and the ability to give rise to right views.) The Song dynasty gentleman Shao Kangjie wrote in a poem: ‘At dawn of every day one stick of incense burn; to Heaven, to Earth, to throne due thanks return. I only ask that every field bear grain, and every man long years of life attain. May the state have wise ministers to keep it strong, and no rebellious son at home do parents wrong. May the four quarters rest, all weapons cease; though I be poor, at heart I shall be at ease.’

From what has been said above, we may know that the mind of the three teachings — Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism — is to teach people to be impartial; therefore we should hold this measure of mind to master ourselves and govern our minds, and never, because of the selfish thoughts of each passing moment, create heavy sin upon heavy sin!
To wreck another’s success and cause him to fail when success is within his grasp.

The word ‘wreck’ has two meanings: one is to destroy, the other is to slander. One who wishes to accomplish merit — whether great merit or small — spares no effort in striving for success; yet I insist on obstructing him, wrecking him, causing him to fail. Such cunning of mind is as venomous as a snake or a scorpion! Mr. Zhen Xishan of the Song dynasty said, ‘When we hear that someone has done a good deed, we should praise him and second his good deed; when we hear that someone has done an evil deed, we must do our utmost to cover it up for him.’ To enable another to succeed, without any loss of one’s own virtue — such was the mind of the ancients; how much less should one dare to wreck the success of one who has already succeeded!

Zeng Xian of the Ming dynasty was in charge of frontier military affairs and wished to recover the Ordos region. The prime minister of the day, Yan Song, who monopolized power and was corrupt, feared that Zeng Xian might recover the Ordos and win great merit; so he seized the opportunity to slander Zeng Xian and Xia Yan before the emperor, saying that they had stirred up conflict on the frontier without authorization. As a result both Zeng Xian and Xia Yan were put to death by the court. Later Yan Song was impeached and reduced to a commoner; and his son Yan Shifan was beheaded.

In the Song dynasty there was a man named Xuan Qiying, of a sinister disposition. When his neighbor’s house was nearly finished, Xuan Qiying, envious that the neighbor’s new house was about to be completed, took advantage of the darkness of night and broke the base of the pillars of the neighbor’s house; at that moment the great beam suddenly fell, and Xuan Qiying was crushed to death on the spot.

Alas! One who wrecks others is in truth wrecking himself! People today, in a matter of business, or in some object, or in affairs such as trade and lending, are ever fond of showing off a quick tongue and wrecking another’s success; such a mind is truly contemptible, and we should know that such a person is destroying himself!
To make others bear the danger while seeking only one’s own safety.

Thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises discuss only one word: mind. Now when I am in the midst of calamity and chaos together with others, I actually want others to bear the danger while I dwell in safety; such a mind has truly lost its original conscience! Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, ‘To avoid danger and seek safety is the ordinary way of human feeling; why then is it detested by Heaven? Heaven does not detest a man’s seeking safety for himself; it detests his making others bear the danger. In the many situations a person passes through in life, there is none without the distinction of safety and danger. If one knows only to seek safety for oneself and pays no heed to the danger of others, then a killing intent has already lain hidden within, and at any time and place there will be the danger of its bursting out. If such scheming could succeed, then all the crafty and deceitful could sleep undisturbed on their high pillows, while those with a kind and generous heart would have no way to live. How could this be the mind of Heaven and Earth? Moreover, the pivot of safety and danger turns like a revolving ring; in the end it will not let those with selfish minds see through it. So what they move toward may instead be the place of danger, and what they avoid may instead be the smooth road. If one can be impartial in mind between self and others, then wherever one goes, one will be safe.’

Li Xu of the Song dynasty was in charge of the military affairs of Yong’an. At that time a band of robbers of great strength had just begun to stir up trouble. Li Xu, fearing that he himself would meet with disaster, used a scheme to recommend his good friend Fan Xing to act in his place in charge of the Yong’an army; so after Fan Xing took up the post, Li Xu was able to leave his residence in Yong’an. Later Fan Xing’s whole family was killed by the robbers. Not long after this, Li Xu was transferred to Lin’an; on the road to Lin’an he met robbers, and Li Xu’s whole family too was killed by them.

Alas! Seeing another in danger, a gentleman will still think of every means to rescue him from his peril; how can one make others face danger while keeping oneself safe? This is the conduct of a mean and ungenerous petty man; and what he obtains is the greatest calamity!
To cut down another’s profit and seek only one’s own gain.

In all the world, only one who benefits others can benefit himself. If a thing benefits oneself while not benefiting others, it is still not true benefit; how much worse is it to diminish another’s profit while taking a greater profit for oneself! Such a person is what is called ‘one who cares only for his own wealth and not for the poverty of others.’ Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, ‘People today, in matters of money, land, houses, and property, often diminish others to benefit themselves in just this way; how could they know that in doing so they are only borrowing a debt from others without writing out an IOU! Though their wealth increases day by day, the term of their life draws nearer and nearer; seen in this light, where is the profit?’

In the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty there were two men, A and B, who were on very good terms. At that time the court was holding the examination to select military candidates, and local officials might recommend one military candidate to the court. A asked the county magistrate to recommend his man, and B asked the assistant prefect to recommend his; and whoever was recommended, if he passed, had to give a gift of fifty taels of gold as a thank-offering. Later A reflected that the magistrate’s prestige was not great enough, and that the man he recommended would certainly fail, whereas the assistant prefect’s prestige was sufficient and the man he recommended would certainly succeed. So, wishing to cut down B’s profit for his own advantage, A devised a plan and said to B, ‘Since the two of us are of one mind, we should share both sweet and bitter. If in the recommendation of military candidates only one of our two men is taken — whether it be your man or mine — we should divide the thank-money equally between us.’ B agreed to A’s proposal. When the results were posted, the man recommended through the assistant prefect had unexpectedly not been taken, while the man recommended through the county magistrate had unexpectedly passed. And the thank-money, which had been sealed up and deposited before the recommendation, was all in B’s keeping, with B responsible for it; A could not go back on his word, and could only mope in silent gloom.

From this story we see that A meant to benefit himself but instead benefited another; and by this principle we know that whenever officials exploit the people, or the rich squeeze interest out of the poor, seeking to fatten themselves by lining their own pockets, in the end there is no one who does not suffer loss himself!
In the exchange of goods, to secretly substitute bad goods for good.

What is called ‘exchanging the bad for the good’ is, for example, taking iron to exchange for gold, using stone to exchange for fine jade, or exchanging cloth for silk and satin; in the eyes of a broad-minded person it is not worth a laugh. But the mind and motive of such a person come close to theft. The Fourth Patriarch said, ‘Outer states, in themselves, have no distinction of fair and foul; the distinction of fair and foul arises from the mind. If the mind did not insist on discriminating, deluded thoughts and attachment would have no way to arise.’ In the Tang dynasty, Dharma Master Wonhyo of Goryeo traveled on foot a thousand li to come to China, wishing to find a master of high understanding to study the Buddha-dharma. One night, because he was hurrying on the road, he slept in a desolate heap of graves. At that time he was both thirsty and weary and wanted to drink water; he saw beside him a pool of clear water, and scooping it up with his bowl he drank it all at one draught, and it felt wonderfully refreshing and good. When day broke and he looked, it was a pool of liquid oozing from a corpse! Dharma Master Wonhyo was at once seized with nausea and vomited up all the water he had drunk the night before; and in that instant he was greatly awakened, saying, ‘The three realms are mind only, the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only; the three realms and the six paths of rebirth are all made by our own mind, and the appearances of all dharmas in the universe are discriminated by our own consciousness. So the feelings of beauty and of repulsion are all our own mind making distinctions; they have nothing whatever to do with the water!’

The great Song literary master Su Dongpo once treasured a piece of fine jade. An official named Zhang Chi came to visit Su Dongpo at his home and asked to see the jade; and seizing the opportunity while admiring it, Zhang Chi secretly substituted a piece of Yan stone for the fine jade. Su Dongpo did not notice at the time; only when he arrived at Huangzhou did he discover that the jade had long since been swapped by Zhang Chi; yet Su Dongpo merely laughed it off. Not long after this, Zhang Chi was demoted by the court and exiled to Taizhou, where he died. Who knows into whose hands that fine jade has now passed!
To set aside public principle for the sake of one’s private mind.

To set aside the right and wrong, the crooked and straight, of public justice for the sake of one’s personal likes and dislikes, favors and grudges: if those in high station set aside the public for the private, then the crooked and the upright cannot be distinguished; and then among friends and neighbors there will be the suspicion of forming cliques, attacking dissenters, and excluding those of different views. If a person sets aside the public for the private, and goes further to love and hate improperly, then even his own family, father and son, the nearest flesh and blood, will become enemies. The harm of being blinded by human feeling is nowhere greater than this! Whether worthy or foolish, noble or base, everyone has this failing, only in different degrees. Knowing the harm of this failing, one should understand principle in order to dissolve one’s own biased temperament, and calm the mind in order to dissolve the guarded depths within one’s heart; one who can do this is a person of great learning and great capacity!

The Song dynasty ministers Zhao Bian and Fan Zhen had come to nurse a grudge against each other because of disagreements over court policy. When Wang Anshi became prime minister, he hated Fan Zhen for having once pointed out his faults to Emperor Shenzong; so when the emperor asked, ‘What sort of man is Fan Zhen?’ Wang Anshi replied, ‘Zhao Bian understands Fan Zhen’s character best of all!’ So the emperor asked Zhao Bian, and Zhao Bian said, ‘Fan Zhen is a loyal minister.’ The emperor asked again, ‘How do you know he is loyal?’ Zhao Bian said, ‘Once when Emperor Renzong was ill and bedridden, Fan Zhen was the first to submit a memorial, requesting that Emperor Renzong designate the crown prince to settle the realm and the people’s hearts. The memorial was presented to Renzong on the nineteenth day, and Fan Zhen waited altogether a hundred days before the memorial was approved. Over this matter Fan Zhen’s hair and beard turned white with anxiety; so if Fan Zhen is not a loyal minister, what is he?’ When Zhao Bian had audience with the emperor and finished speaking, he withdrew; and Wang Anshi reproached him, saying, ‘Are you not at enmity with Fan Zhen?’ Zhao Bian said, ‘I dare not set aside public justice for the sake of private grudge.’

Formerly Kong Yi, the magistrate of Luoyang, placed a brazier in the courtyard of his office, and every letter seeking a favor or intercession he threw into the brazier to burn, without even looking at it. He said, ‘The magistrate is closest of all to the people, and in official life there are bound to be many requests and intercessions. If I comply, the people will suffer harm; if I do not comply, I cannot avoid offending people. The only way is that when a letter of intercession reaches my hands, I do not open it but at once throw it into the brazier to burn. For my part, I do not know what the request concerns; and for the one making the request, he will not be offended either. For the right and wrong, the crooked and straight, of public principle all have a fixed standard, and the judging of cases has the basis of law — how can one set aside the public for the private?’ Later Kong Yi’s son passed the imperial examination as a presented scholar at the age of nineteen.
To steal another’s skill and take it as one’s own.

For example, to steal another’s essay and think it one’s own essay; to steal another’s plan and think it one’s own plan; to steal another’s merit and think it one’s own merit; to steal a teacher’s instruction and think it one’s own insight — all these are acts of deceiving oneself and others, and will surely bring condemnation.

In the Zhou dynasty, when Mount Liang collapsed, the ruler of Jin summoned the grand officer Bo Zong to learn the circumstances of the landslide. On his way to audience with the ruler, Grand Officer Bo Zong met a cart driver and asked him, ‘Have you heard any news lately?’ The driver replied, ‘Mount Liang has collapsed, and the earth and rocks that fell have dammed up the river, so that the water no longer flows! I hear that the ruler of Jin is about to summon Grand Officer Bo Zong over this matter to discuss how to solve it.’ Bo Zong asked the driver, ‘Then how should it be solved?’ The driver said, ‘Very simply: if the ruler of Jin himself leads the civil and military officials to Mount Liang to weep and make offerings, the river water will flow again.’ Bo Zong took the driver’s suggestion and reported it to the ruler of Jin; and after the ruler adopted and carried it out, the river water began to flow. The ruler of Jin asked Bo Zong, ‘How did you come to know this method?’ Bo Zong replied, ‘I thought of it myself!’ When Confucius heard of it he said, ‘Bo Zong, that man, is about to have his line cut off! For he has stolen another’s good deed and made it his own.’ In the end Bo Zong indeed met with a violent death, and his office of grand officer was cut off.

Alas! Bo Zong merely stole a single sentence from another, and even so suffered such a severe chastisement from Heaven; how much more so for other, worse deeds — their retribution need not be spoken of to be known!
To conceal another’s good deeds so that others do not know of them.

The Buddhist sutras say, ‘The one word “good” is the most able to bring to fulfillment all the vows and aspirations of people in the world.’ Therefore if a person has even one good word or one good deed, we should praise it; and we should even fear that our praise is not enough, that we may fail to make his good words and good deeds shine abroad. By doing so we not only accomplish his own fair repute, but can also stir the good thoughts of others; and we can cause everyone to spread and encourage one another, so that those who do good will be more and more numerous. This is truly a joy — why should one conceal and cover it up? Therefore the person who conceals another’s good deeds must have no love of goodness at all in his heart, and may even harbor jealousy; and only for this reason is he unwilling to make known another’s virtue in doing good, fearing perhaps that it would throw his own wickedness into relief. Such a person is an inauspicious person in the world!
